names.name: paśyantī, the supreme station of speech

descriptions: without beginning or end, the principle of the Word, imperishable, appearing as things (VP 1.1)
one, appearing as many through its powers, though not separate from them (VP 1.2)
the single seed of all, existing as enjoyer, enjoyed and enjoyment (VP 1.4)
the Being that all words finally denote (VP 3.1–3.2)
negations: paśyantī is undivided, with all sequence withdrawn (Vṛtti on VP 1.142)
relation_to_self: Consciousness is of the nature of speech: if the eternal word-nature of awareness departed, light would not illumine (VP 1.124 Iyer); the Word is the inner consciousness of beings.
relation_to_world: The world is an appearance (vivarta) of the Word-principle, proceeding through its time-power; the universe evolved first from the Vedic metres (VP 1.1, 1.3, 1.120 Iyer).
caveat: The grammarians hold a single ultimate but not a personal Lord. Their identification of the Word (paśyantī) with Brahman is rejected by the Kashmir Śaivas (who place parā vāk above paśyantī), by Buddhist and Jain critics, and by Mīmāṃsā (which denies sphoṭa); whether Bhartṛhari's 'vivarta' means illusory appearance in the later Advaita sense is disputed by scholars.

names.name: rasa (relish) — as the 'twin' of tasting Brahman
brahmāsvāda-sahodara (twin of the taste of Brahman)

descriptions: arising from the predominance of sattva, undivided, self-luminous, made of bliss and consciousness, untouched by any other object, the twin of tasting Brahman, whose life is supermundane wonder (SD 3.2–3)
for Abhinavagupta: the relish of one's own consciousness, universalized and at rest (viśrānti)
negations: not identical with tasting Brahman: it depends on determinants and lasts while the work is enjoyed (implied in 'sahodara')
relation_to_self: In rasa the spectator relishes his own consciousness freed from personal limitation (Abhinavagupta); in śānta the stable emotion is knowledge of the self (tattvajñāna).
relation_to_world: Drama imitates the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.107); rasa is 'supermundane' (alaukika), neither real nor unreal in the ordinary sense.
caveat: Poetics is not a darśana and does not itself posit an ultimate. It compares aesthetic relish with realization, explicitly as a 'twin', not an identity; each author supplies the ultimate from his own school (Abhinavagupta: Trika Śaivism; Viśvanātha: Vedānta; Rūpa Gosvāmī: Kṛṣṇa). Advaita treats the relish of bliss in samādhi (rasāsvāda) as an obstacle (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.45), a contrast to be kept.

names.name: Brahman, consciousness-bliss, called Īśvara and liṅga (ŚR 1.2.4)

descriptions: the consciousness of all beings, unfolded as the world; bliss, without a second (ŚR 1.3.1)
Brahman is consciousness-bliss, self-luminous, stainless, called Īśvara and liṅga, unborn, all-pervading, changeless, formless, all-powerful and omniscient (ŚR 1.2.4–5)
Brahmā, Janārdana, the supreme Śakti and Maheśvara are forms of nāda (Bṛhaddeśī 17–18)
relation_to_self: The jīvas are parts of Brahman, like sparks of fire, conditioned by beginningless avidyā and bound by karma; they are not different from the self (ŚR 1.2.5–6, 1.2.11).
relation_to_world: Brahman creates the world by its power as gold becomes earrings — or, 'others say', through avidyā as a rope appears as a snake; Śārṅgadeva reports both views (ŚR 1.2.11–12).
caveat: The music treatises borrow their metaphysics (Vedāntic and Śaiva) and record rival views of creation without deciding them; 'nāda-brahman' names the ultimate as approached through sound, not a separate doctrine of the ultimate.

names.name: Śabda-brahman = the consciousness of all beings

descriptions: the supreme Lord, splendid with being, consciousness and bliss, with parts (sakala), from whom Śakti, nāda and bindu arise (ŚT 1.7)
śabda-brahman is the consciousness of all beings (ŚT 1.13)
negations: śabda-brahman is neither the word nor its meaning, both of which are insentient (ŚT 1.12–13)
relation_to_self: The same consciousness dwells in each body as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.14).
relation_to_world: The world of words and of things unfolds from the supreme through Śakti, nāda, bindu and the fifty letters (ŚT 1.7–16).
caveat: The mantra manuals serve worshippers of many deities (Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya) and adopt a Śaiva–Śākta cosmogony of sound; they are not a separate darśana and would defer to the metaphysics of the worshipper's own school.
